summary: Postmortem follow-up on a production incident on 2027-02-28 where Apex experienced elevated latencies and cost spikes due to a cache invalidation + autoscaler interaction. We reviewed root cause, immediate mitigations, and agreed on reliability improvements and next steps (RCA deck, benchmark, runbook updates, and tighter alerts).
transcript: [00:00] Ari Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. we'll give about 45 mins. quick intros?
[00:10] Lena Ortiz: Lena here, CTO at Apex. thanks. Samir and Dana with me.
[00:18] Samir Patel: Samir, SRE manager. we pulled data and want to understand the RCA and fixes.
[00:25] Ari Chen: Great. Maya from Redwood will walk through the timeline and root cause.
[00:33] Maya Rao: hi all, I'll jump in. quick note - transcript auto captions may have odd words like KV cash instead of cache so forgive that, ok?

[00:40] Maya Rao: Timeline: on 2027-02-28 around 14:12 UTC, Apex hit a traffic spike from a partner batch job. within 3 mins we saw an increase in request queueing and 95th latency degraded from ~120ms to 2.4s.
[01:05] Dana Kim: It was really visible on our dashboards, lots of timeouts for the shipment ETA endpoint.

[01:12] Maya Rao: Root cause (high level): a KV-cache invalidation event coincided with the autoscaler's scaling cooldown. The cache flush increased origin load, autoscaler misread the queue metric as transient and didn't scale aggressively, which caused request bursts to fall back to a higher-latency fallback path (larger model variants) and we also saw request retries amplify traffic.
[01:45] Omar Ruiz: we saw cost spike because the fallback model is more expensive per token, that surprised our finance folks.
[01:52] Ari Chen: yes, cost spike reported ~3.1x for the 18-minute window. Maya, can you expand on the autoscaler behavior?

[02:00] Maya Rao: Sure — the autoscaler uses the queue length over 60s windows. there was a cooldown because a previous scale event finished 40s before the spike; the cooldown suppressed a second scale-up. also our heuristic ignored short-lived cache misses if they recovered in <90s, but this event pushed into sustained decompression of the model kv state.
[02:30] Samir Patel: were there any errors in the model serving stack? logs show some KV timeouts and a couple 'model load failed' artifacts.

[02:38] Maya Rao: Yes, there were transient model load failures when the system attempted to spin up additional model replicas under memory pressure. this caused retries; some RPCs returned 503s for a short period.
[02:50] Dana Kim: question: could dedicated capacity have prevented this?

[02:55] Maya Rao: Dedicated would provide reserved GPU pools and avoid noisy neighbor interference and faster scale characteristics; but if the cache invalidation pattern is in the app and causes origin load, dedicated helps but proper cache management and warm starts are also required.
[03:20] Lena Ortiz: Our concern is predictability during peak jobs. we need concrete SLOs and failover behavior that don't blow budget.

[03:30] Ari Chen: Understood. we can present a cost/latency tradeoff: dedicated capacity reservation vs hosted with stricter routing policies and pre-warmed replicas. we'll include pricing impact from the incident.

[03:45] Maya Rao: immediate mitigations we deployed during the incident: 1) temporary rate limit on the partner batch job, 2) forced cache warming with histogram-backed prefetch, 3) manual scale-up override to add model replicas, 4) rollback of a recent network config that increased cold-starts.
[04:10] Samir Patel: Which of those are permanent? we need durable fixes not manual ops.

[04:15] Maya Rao: Agreed — permanent remediations: update autoscaler thresholds, add an edge-level circuit breaker for big batch jobs, implement predictive cache warming for large TTL changes, and more granular cost-based fallback policies to prevent expensive model fallbacks.
[04:40] Omar Ruiz: predictive warming — does that risk warming unnecessarily and wasting compute?

[04:45] Maya Rao: We'll tune heuristics: only pre-warm when we detect >X% sustained increase in request prefix traffic or when upstream signals indicate a batch window starting. conservative pre-warm reduces wasted cycles.
[05:00] Dana Kim: on observability, we want better tracing into KV cache evictions. right now it's opaque in our stack.
[05:07] Maya Rao: We're adding span-level tracing for cache hits/misses and a dedicated dashboard for cache churn per route. we'll also surface predicted eviction windows.
[05:20] Samir Patel: can get an SLO that if 95th latency > 500ms we auto-failover to cached responses instead of heavier model?

[05:28] Ari Chen: We Can implement a staged fallback: cached last-known good responses for certain endpoints, degrade to embeddings-level answer for non-critical calls — we'll define per-route fail policies.
[05:40] Lena Ortiz: Security question — were any customer data logs sent to third-party during the incident?
[05:46] Maya Rao: No evidence of exfiltration. all retries and fallbacks remained within the same VPC for your deployment. we'll share the audit logs. we also have KMS/HSM keys unaffected.
[06:00] Samir Patel: we'd like the SOC2/ISO evidence and audit log slice for the incident window.
[06:05] Ari Chen: noted — we'll attach the compliance docs and the log slice as part of the postmortem package.

[06:15] Maya Rao: Next, a quick deep-dive on the RCA timeline (high-res). [06:20] starting 14:12 UTC — cache flush triggered by a config push from your ops team that set TTL to 0 for a route, that caused mass invalidations.
[06:40] Omar Ruiz: yes, that config push coincided with a deployment; we didn't realize TTL set to zero — that's on us.
[06:50] Samir Patel: (laugh) the change was rolled by a temp engineer. we'll fix gating.
[06:55] Maya Rao: No blame — this highlights controls. mitigations include requiring canary for config changes that touch cache TTLs, and an API guard that prevents TTL=0 without code review.
[07:15] Dana Kim: can Redwood enforce a guard on the API? like a pre-commit hook?
[07:20] Maya Rao: We can add a server-side validation that rejects TTL=0 without an explicit override flag and an audit trail. we'll propose the implementation in the deck.
[07:35] Ari Chen: Let's move to reliability improvements: runbook, testing, and alerts. Devon has an initial runbook draft.

[07:42] Devon Park: Hi. The runbook will include detection signals (cache eviction rate, queue length, model load failures), escalation steps (rate limit partner, manual scale, contact Redwood SE), and test playbooks to run quarterly.
[07:58] Samir Patel: we want an automated smoke test that runs after config pushes to detect large cache evictions.
[08:04] Devon Park: We'll work on a synthetic test that uses a set of key prefixes and measures hitrate delta post-deploy. can coordinate with your CI.
[08:20] Lena Ortiz: also want to run a dedicated capacity pilot to see consistent latency under our known peaks.
[08:26] Ari Chen: Good plan — SE to provision a dedicated test pool for one week. we'll measure throughput/latency and calculate commit sizing.

[08:35] Maya Rao: During the incident we also saw model-variant fallback logic choose a larger model because the smaller quantized variant had incomplete kv-compatibility; we'll fix variant selection rules to prefer cheaper but compatible models or a degraded response.
[08:55] Omar Ruiz: what's the timeline to fix variant selection?
[08:58] Maya Rao: quick config patch in 3 business days to change fallback order, code change for compatibility checks in 2 weeks.
[09:10] Samir Patel: can you provide a retro doc that includes cost numbers? we need to show finance the budget hit.
[09:15] Ari Chen: yes — action: Ari will share a line-item showing the incident cost delta and expected recurring cost if patterns repeat.
[09:25] Dana Kim: about alerts — current alerts only trigger after 5m sustained high latency. can we reduce that?
[09:31] Maya Rao: we'll add a fast-path alert for cache-churn anomalies at 30s and a secondary alert for queue growth at 90s.
[09:40] Lena Ortiz: anything else on compliance? we may need log retention changes for audits.
[09:45] Ari Chen: We can offer extended retention as an add-on; we'll include pricing options in the follow-up.

[09:55] Devon Park: Summarizing next steps: postmortem deck (Redwood), log slices and compliance docs (Redwood), traffic traces (Apex), dedicated test pool (Redwood), runbook drafts (Redwood + Apex), and pilot schedule.
[10:10] Samir Patel: thanks. can we have a follow-up sync after you share the deck? 1 week out?
[10:15] Ari Chen: Yes — propose 2027-03-10 for a 30-min check-in. we'll send calendar invite.
[10:22] Lena Ortiz: appreciate the thoroughness. one last question — will the autoscaler cooldown logic be adjustable per-customer?
[10:29] Maya Rao: yes, we'll expose per-tenant autoscaler tuning in Redwood Console so you can set shorter cooldowns for time-sensitive routes.
[10:38] Omar Ruiz: great. Also, can we get a test harness to simulate the partner batch job?
[10:43] Maya Rao: SE will provide a harness and sample traffic generator. action item listed.
[10:50] Ari Chen: ok wrapping up — Devon, Ari, Maya will compile the postmortem and action list and send by EOD 2027-03-03. Apex to send traces by 2027-03-04. we'll reconvene 2027-03-10.
[10:58] Lena Ortiz: thanks all. good meeting.
[11:02] Samir Patel: thanks.
